title: Workers trade wage gains against layoff risk, and incomplete insurance can suppress mobility
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35580; representative survey of employed U.S. workers plus a general-equilibrium search model with wage and unemployment-risk job ladders
geography: United States; employed workers and modeled labor market

observations.period: Survey and model results; working paper issued August 2026

denominator.unit: custom representative survey of employed U.S. workers; exact respondent denominator not disclosed in abstract

security_premium.unit: percent pay raise demanded for each additional percentage point of annual unemployment risk in a new job

complete_markets_mobility.unit: percent modeled increase in job mobility under complete markets

complete_markets_productivity.unit: percent modeled productivity increase under complete markets

ui_productivity.unit: percent modeled productivity increase from unemployment insurance in the paper's mechanism

ui_tradeoff.value: unemployment insurance encourages employed workers to accept risky, higher-productivity offers while also increasing job loss and unemployment

observations.method: The paper elicits employed workers' wage-safety indifference curves in a representative survey and embeds the result in a general-equilibrium search model with two-dimensional job ladders, risk-averse workers, incomplete self-insurance, and on/off-the-job search.
observations.uncertainty: The paper is a working paper. The survey estimate is stated at the population level but the abstract does not disclose the sample denominator or subgroup estimates; modeled mobility, productivity, and unemployment effects depend on the search-model structure and calibration. A stated willingness-to-pay for security is not a realized job choice or household outcome.
observations.subgroup: Employed U.S. workers; the abstract reports that incomplete markets and borrowing constraints matter but does not provide the subgroup denominator or full heterogeneity estimates.
observations.counterinterpretation: Workers may value security for family, health, location, benefits, identity, or employer-specific reasons not captured by annual unemployment risk. UI can alter search, take-up, vacancy filling, and firm behavior in ways that differ from the model; safer jobs may also offer lower training or advancement.

boundary: This record adds a measured wage-for-security trade-off and a modeled insurance-to-mobility mechanism. It does not establish actual job switching, household security, worker voice, or universal effects of unemployment insurance in observed administrative data.
